item.title: Rubio could be the GOP's answer for 2028, but Congress may complicate his path
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Newly ascendant Democrats on Capitol Hill aren't planning to make it easy for Marco Rubio to ride to the GOP's rescue in 2028. The secretary of State's appeal to Latinos and relatively strong standing in Washington may offer Republicans, battered by this week's midterm elections, hope that they can bridge their internal divides and hold onto the White House. "The number of people who want to draft Secretary of State Marco Rubio is staggering," former GOP House Speaker Newt Gingrich wrote Wednesday on social media . But Democratic lawmakers are likely to make Rubio a top target for oversight and other hearings in the new Congress — grilling him on the Iran war, legally questionable strikes on alleged drug boats , deals related to Venezuelan oil and more, according to a House Democratic aide and a Senate Democratic aide familiar with the discussions. Similarly aggressive scrutiny from Republican lawmakers helped tarnish former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's image during the years before she ran for president in 2016. Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser, has largely avoided the criticism aimed at President Donald Trump's Iran war and other major crises — but that doesn't absolve him of responsibility for administration failures, Democrats said. "He belongs near the top of the list of people who must answer to congressional oversight," said the Democratic Senate aide, who, like others, was granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive issue. Democrats are still mapping out their accountability strategy, so any plans at the moment are tenuous. They stress that their actions are not about 2028 but about fulfilling Congress' oversight duties, which they say Republicans failed to do during their time in charge. Democrats also are more interested in other Trump-related figures, especially Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — a fellow rumored 2028 hopeful — who is facing a possible House impeachment vote this month. Rubio, meanwhile, has downplayed talk that he would run for president. He told The New York Times on Thursday that he planned to serve as chief diplomat for Trump's full term, even as stories circulated in some news organizations that he was considering quitting. But staying in office for any length of time makes it more likely Democrats will pursue oversight of his actions. It also puts him at a potential disadvantage compared with some 2028 hopefuls who have never served in the administration or, such as with Vice President JD Vance, are elsewhere in its ranks. Democrats in Congress have a clear line of authority to compel Rubio — a Senate-confirmed Cabinet department chief — to testify, regardless of whether he remains in or leaves the administration. Should he refuse to testify, that gives Democrats even more ammunition for criticism. In contrast, White House personnel, including the vice president, have traditionally been exempt from being hauled up to the Hill. And the Trump administration is likely to invoke such traditions, executive privilege or other measures to shield its staff from Hill hearings. Asked about Democrats' planned oversight moves, a State Department official touted Rubio's leadership in executing Trump's foreign policy agenda. "We will not only defend our record but proudly tout the historic foreign policy successes of the Trump Administration," said the official, granted anonymity to share how the department would respond to Democrats' demand for testimony. The White House insisted Trump would be happy to partner with the same people he has antagonized for two years. He is "willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." Since the election drubbing, other potential 2028 candidates have tried to distance themselves from Trump's unpopular actions. Vance released a statement blaming the Iran war as the main reason for the loss. Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who ran for president in 2024, gave a lengthy interview in which he criticized Trump policies and said the midterms were an "extinction-level" event for the party. Rubio has said little publicly since Tuesday's election, although he acknowledged to the Times that higher gas prices likely affected the vote. But he added that Trump deserved credit for making an unpopular choice on Iran. That loyalty to the president has won him favor within the White House and among many of Trump's hardcore MAGA voters. Despite his close alignment with the president, Rubio has also managed to cultivate appeal with more traditional Republicans, who believe he could help strengthen conventional conservatives. "He'd make an excellent candidate and help the Republican Party return to small 'c' conservative values, in line with where the electorate is," said Ludovic Hood, a former longtime U.S. diplomat who recently left the State Department. "He's a savvy politician, a great communicator." Prior to the election, Rubio held to State Department tradition and avoided the campaign until the final days when Trump briefly lured him onto the trail. Asked about a potential Rubio bid, the State Department official echoed his denials, saying "those who reported this will be mocked in the coming weeks when Secretary Rubio is still proudly serving under President Trump." Matthew Bartlett, a GOP strategist and former Trump appointee at the State Department, downplayed the likelihood of a Rubio campaign launch, saying he faced a nearly impossible task of disentangling from Trump's foreign policy failures. "If you're in this Cabinet, you're wearing cement shoes," Bartlett said. Even if Rubio did launch a 2028 bid, he's ill-equipped to respond to voter scrutiny over the war, Bartlett said. "Diplomatic talk may be appreciated among those that wear white wingtips," he said, "but in the town halls, straight talk is appropriate, and I'm not sure that you can give a straight answer on Iran right now." But Rubio has changed his mind about whether to run for office before. Buzz Jacobs, who advised Rubio during his 2016 presidential campaign, said that if Rubio decides to leave soon to run for president, he "has to navigate a careful exit from the administration, so it doesn't look like he's abandoning his duties at a time of war," while also ensuring he has the time he needs to fundraise and build a campaign. Unusually for someone in his position, Rubio has taken a back seat on major portfolios, including the wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza. Vance and envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have played bigger roles in those crises. Rubio has instead focused largely on Latin America. He's overseeing U.S. efforts to topple the regime in Cuba, his ancestral homeland. He's also the main U.S. interlocutor for what's left of the regime in Venezuela after the Trump administration captured autocrat Nicolás Maduro. Rubio may seem less politically scarred by the administration's struggles in places such as Iran. But some critics question why he didn't do more to course correct given his titles and responsibilities. Rubio's role as national security adviser in particular means he's supposed to coordinate major foreign policy moves across the government. On Iran in particular, Rubio is "trying to keep his hands clean on this because he probably knows it's a politically bad issue. But he is responsible even if he's not out there running this every day," the Democratic House aide said. In March, Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the likely incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, pushed a failed motion to subpoena Rubio to appear before the panel to talk about the Iran war. Nearly half of Democratic respondents to a pre-midterm POLITICO poll said they wanted to see the House impeach Rubio. Some Rubio supporters noted that conditions could change. "If they can bring the Iran war to a successful conclusion between now and when people may vote, then Marco Rubio will look like an absolute genius," Jacobs said. Some of Rubio's efforts in Latin America might be cast as potential successes, including the removal of Maduro from his perch in Caracas. The Latin America moves in particular might please many of his fellow Latinos in Florida and beyond. Latino votes proved critical in the midterm results this week. But Democrats are questioning Rubio's long-term vision in Latin America, too. Of particular interest is Rubio's role in Trump's efforts to battle drug cartels, which include U.S. military strikes on boats that some legal experts and senior Democrats say could amount to war crimes. There are also concerns about business deals the Trump administration and its allies are striking in Venezuela. Curt Mills, executive director of the anti-interventionist American Conservative magazine and a vocal critic of the Iran war, marveled at Rubio's seeming invisibility in recent days. "Is Rubio going to say that this midterm was about the war? Is he going to say anything? Is he going to do anything? Or is he just focused on himself and Latin America?" Mills asked. item.title: Stephen Miller pushed for 3,000 ICE arrests a day. Now he's Trump's chief of staff.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller , who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations. Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term. The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies. Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025. During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018. He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual refugee admissions ceiling, ultimately setting it at 15,000 for fiscal year 2021, a record low at the time. Under former President Barack Obama, the ceiling was 110,000 for fiscal year 2017. Miller also advocated penalizing legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it harder for them to obtain citizenship. In Mr. Trump's second term, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day. In May 2025, Miller publicly demanded a dramatic increase in daily arrests, placing pressure on ICE leadership and expanding enforcement beyond immigrants who had been convicted of serious crimes. He also proposed that the National Guard be deployed to support mass deportations. Miller's arrest targets were part of a sweeping expansion of enforcement in communities, workplaces and immigration courts. Detentions of immigrants without criminal histories rose sharply , and increased ICE activity sparked protests across the country. The longtime Trump adviser also championed the use of a wartime law — the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — to bypass due process and quickly deport alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held in a notorious maximum-security prison, known as CECOT. The deportations set off a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the government from immediately deporting the Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal. As part of the administration's deportation efforts, Miller has supported an aggressive expansion of third-country deportations . The administration has deported immigrants to countries where they have no citizenship or family ties, including several African nations . In May 2025, Miller said the administration was actively considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court. At a March 2026 conference in Miami, Miller argued that military force, rather than traditional criminal law enforcement alone, was needed to defeat cartels. Miller appeared alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office this summer as he signed executive orders to refuse citizenship to some children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier executive order aiming to end birthright citizenship. item.title: Trump officials weigh major overhaul of National Park and Fish and Wildlife services
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is considering a major reorganization of the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, according to internal documents reviewed by The Washington Post. Staff are meeting this week and next to discuss a “realignment” of the two agencies, the documents show. One meeting regarding the National Park Service will discuss “pending duty station changes,” referring to the locations where staff report to work. But the documents do not specify whether certain offices would be closed or moved, or whether any employees would be fired. The Interior Department, which oversees the agencies, did not respond to a request for comment. Get Climate Coach newsletter News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free Public land advocates fear that the changes could further hurt agencies that have already seen major staffing cuts since Trump began efforts to shrink the federal government by hundreds of thousands of employees last year. “I think from their perspective, it seems as though that they’re trying to find efficiencies by consolidating staff within DOI that maybe served different functions across these agencies,” said Ed Stierli, vice president of government affairs at the National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy group. “But I think in reality, it just seems to be causing more confusion and chaos. ” While the administration has considered differing plans to overhaul the Park Service since last year, including one reported in September by the Washington Sun, plans to reorganize the Fish and Wildlife Service are more recent. Fish and Wildlife manages more than 500 National Wildlife Refuges across the country, spanning 93 million acres. A Fish and Wildlife Service report published on Friday recommends the agency “reduce headquarters and regional office staffing and reallocate positions to refuge operations, prioritizing the people needed to manage habitat, maintain facilities, support public access and protect resources.” An internal communication to Fish and Wildlife Service staff on Friday, reviewed by The Post, states that the recommendations in the report “give us a path forward” and that “our next responsibility is to turn them into practical actions.” In March, the administration initiated a reorganization of the U.S. Forest Service, which includes relocating its headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City and hundreds of employees with it. The plan would also close some research stations and regional offices as it transitions to state offices. A judge has put that plan on hold , as well as a wider reorganization of the Agriculture Department that oversees it, amid legal challenges. Most Read From The Washington Post Stephen Miller’s promotion angers industries reeling from immigration enforcement Stephen Miller is named new White House chief of staff as Susie Wiles departs Hegseth draws fire after using government resources for partisan video Two more DOJ officials resign, including head of national security division Trump ally declines to back Hegseth when asked whether he should be replaced At the Park Service, the administration has withheld millions in funding and cut Park Service staff by about a quarter, sometimes leading to long lines, fewer tours and dirty bathrooms at parks. “When you talk about changing duty stations for example, are they just trying to cripple this agency?” Stierli asked. “Why would you try and sow chaos into an agency that is already stretched well beyond capacity trying to fulfill its mission?” Bill Wade, executive director of the Association of National Park Rangers, which represents current and former Park Service employees, said that agency employees have had to live with the uncertainty and stress that major restructuring might be coming, possibly including layoffs, since the launch of the DOGE Service last year. Based on the limited information about the current reorganization being considered, “it’s too little to try to determine what the impact would be on the service or employees,” Wade said. It is unclear whether the current reorganization plans for the National Park Service had been significantly revised from earlier proposals. Layoff plans last year at the National Park Service, which have not been independently verified by The Post, were ultimately never carried out. Stierli said that the administration appeared to “pump the brakes” on the plans two months ago, but it may now be feeling a new sense of urgency to restructure the agency with Democrats about to take control of Congress. “Come January, you’re going have a new Congress who’s very eager to do oversight and pry into the National Park Service to look and see how staff are being organized, where is the budget for the Park Service going,” Stierli said. In spending bills, congressional Democrats could write in provisions demanding approval over any restructuring in agencies, or at least to be notified, he said. “We’re certainly hopeful that Congress uses this oversight power here, because I think what’s highly unusual is there’s been zero transparency,” Stierli added. “When there is zero transparency, it creates this confusion.” This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://www.washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2026/11/07/trump-officials-consider-revamping-national-park-service-fish-wildlife-service/

item.title: Wisconsin trooper released from ICE custody after 'dramatic experience'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A 21-year-old South African-born Wisconsin State Patrol trooper who was detained Nov. 5 by federal immigration agents was released from custody Nov. 6, according to his attorney. Attorney Marc Christopher confirmed to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who was traveling to visit family with a valid work permit, had been released from the Dodge County Jail and was awaiting a ride from his supervisor, the head trooper in Tomah. Christopher said Van Der Merwe was released under an order of supervision, which requires him to periodically check in with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He will also likely be subject to electronic monitoring, potentially through an application on his cellphone rather than an ankle bracelet. Christopher said he plans to speak with Van Der Merwe to discuss the next steps in his case. He expects Van Der Merwe will eventually share his experience publicly but wants to give him time to readjust following his release. "I just told him I wanted him to get back, get reacclimated, just get settled, because I know he's gone through a very dramatic experience," Christopher said. Van Der Merwe came to the U.S. from South Africa with his family on visas at age 14, Christopher said. His family has been waiting seven years for their asylum case to be heard. Earlier, Christopher slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for detaining a Wisconsin law enforcement officer who has permission to work, saying he was "flabbergasted" by the agents' decision to use its resources to target Van Der Merwe. "I almost can't even believe that they would be so brazen as to do this. But they are," Christopher said. "There's no reason for them to detain him other than to indiscriminately pick up as many people as they can." Van Der Merwe, who lived in New Mexico with his family, wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but could not because he was not a permanent resident, Christopher said. He graduated with a degree in criminal justice in New Mexico, then researched states where he could do similar work with his status and found Wisconsin. Van Der Merwe was living in Onalaska and working in Tomah for the Wisconsin State Patrol over the past year. His work authorization is valid until 2030. Attorney disputes ICE's assertion about legal status ICE's argument is that Van Der Merwe – as a teenager in the U.S. with his family – overstayed his visitor's visa. "He entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019. In defiance of our nation’s laws, he overstayed his admission," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement. "Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the U.S." Christopher pushed back on that assertion. "That is just absurd and ridiculous," Christopher said. "They've been here lawfully. They have been waiting for their application to be adjudicated and to be decided by immigration." The family, who are White South Africans, had applied for asylum on the grounds they were persecuted. A family member had been attacked, Christopher said. Van Der Merwe did not decide to come to the U.S. himself, as he was brought by his parents, and he chose a career in law enforcement to serve his new country, Christopher said. ICE agents detained him Nov. 5 at the Dane County Regional Airport just after he went through security, Christopher said. He was traveling to visit his family in New Mexico. Agents handcuffed him, shackled his legs and put him in a van and drove him to Dodge County Jail, which holds ICE detainees. Christopher said it seems that the Transportation Security Administration tipped off ICE when he bought his ticket, and agents met Van Der Merwe at the airport. Christopher has heard of ICE making arrests at the Milwaukee and Appleton airports through similar tip-offs, he said. Lawyer hopes Congress changes the way ICE can operate Under the Trump administration, ICE has not been setting bond for detainees voluntarily unless a judge orders it. Trump administration policy changes have made many detainees ineligible to even seek bond and leave detention. Christopher said he hopes Wisconsin's congressional delegation takes note of the case and institutes changes to the way ICE can operate. He was critical that ICE would use its resources to arrest Van Der Merwe, then hold him in custody. "You're going to use your resources to go after this guy? You're going to use our tax dollars to detain this guy? It doesn't make any sense," Christopher said. As part of its summer surge in street arrests in Milwaukee, ICE arrested a 20-year-old Milwaukee man, Giovanni Sosa, who had lived in the U.S. since age 4 . In detaining him, ICE gave him paperwork that said – at age 4 – he had overstayed his visa. Sosa spent a month in detention at the Dodge County Jail as he waited for the chance to post bond. Sophie Carson is a general assignment reporter who reports on religion and faith, immigrants and refugees and more. Contact her at scarson@gannett.com or 920-323-5758. item.title: Trump's grip on his party is in question as Republicans reel from the midterm wipeout
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans aren't holding back. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis described this week's elections as an “extinction-level event” for the GOP. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz likened it to a “Watergate-level repudiation.” Former Vice President Mike Pence called it a “reckoning.” For all the apocalyptic talk emerging from a midterm that relegated Republicans to their thinnest ranks on Capitol Hill in decades, there's little agreement on how the party should move forward. A return to the bedrock fiscal and national security conservatism that defined Republicans under President Ronald Reagan risks alienating the more hard-line conservatives welcomed into the party under President Donald Trump under the “Make America Great Again” banner. But leaning even further into Trump's coarse brand of politics could lead to more voter rejection. “We have soul-searching to do," Alex Latcham, the executive director of the Senate Leadership Fund, which spent $810 million to support Republicans, said in an interview. “We need to first understand and honestly admit why we just endured a wipeout of this magnitude. And then we have to regroup and agree to a path forward.” GOP faces questions about Trump's future role As has been the case for the past decade, the central question is the role Trump will play in shaping the party's future. His insistence on loyalty reached a zenith this year as he intervened in GOP primaries and pressed voters to make the elections a referendum on his second term. He held dozens of rallies in the final weeks of the campaign for candidates, most of whom lost their races. Since Tuesday's election, he's refused to acknowledge any responsibility, placing blame on the candidates. His public events have focused on his pet projects in Washington, which have proven unpopular with voters. On Friday, he elevated Stephen Miller , the architect of some of his most contentious policies, to White House chief of staff. In an interview, Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt , a Republican, said the election results were “shocking” but that Trump could still steer the conversation around issues such as immigration. The governor described the GOP's current dynamic as a natural process for a party whose leader is deep in his second term. “It just tells you that the American people, after 10 years, they're pretty much tired of whoever's in office,” Stitt said. “I think people want a little more stability. They want people to be nice to people, to say, 'Hey, we’re all Americans.'” Others were more blunt. Longtime conservative commentator Tucker Carlson said the midterms marked “the end of the Trump era." John Sununu, a Republican who lost his bid for a Senate seat in New Hampshire, blamed Trump. "It seems like he or his family is in on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington,” Sununu told John Kasich, a former Republican congressman from Ohio, on SiriusXM. “Those two things, I think, caused people to say, ‘You know, I just can’t vote for a Republican while he’s still in office.’” Republican infighting is likely to intensify The GOP infighting is poised to intensify quickly. When Republicans return to Capitol Hill next week, they'll have to choose between Reps. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Jim Jordan of Ohio to lead the party in the House. They may weigh whether to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . There could also be tough votes on defense spending and keeping the federal government open after Dec. 11. Already a leadership fight is brewing at the Republican National Committee, where there are early conversations about limiting Trump’s influence in picking the next chair. KC Crosbie, currently the co-chair, circulated a letter this week calling the midterms a “serious setback” and announcing plans to run for chair at the committee’s January meeting in Arizona. Trump announced his support Friday for the party's current chair, Joe Gruters. That's to say nothing of the emerging contest for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. Vice President JD Vance , seen as a leading contender, will likely face a broad range of opponents if he enters the race. Stitt is among the Republicans calling for a “big open primary.” “I don't think we should crown anybody,” he said. There will be pressure to revive the coalition of voters, particularly Latinos, who have lifted the party to success in previous elections but swung to Democrats this week. Former Rep. Carlos Curbelo, R-Fla., said he thought Secretary of State Marco Rubio is best positioned to win Latinos. “The two main constituencies that Republicans have to quickly regain are white suburban voters and Hispanic voters,” Curbelo said in an interview. “Vance was out on the campaign trail this year and it doesn't appear that he was able to move the needle in terms of Hispanic voters.” A representative for Vance didn't comment on that characterization. Broad election fallout for the GOP Still, the fallout for the GOP is broad, according to The AP Voter Poll , an expansive survey of about 80,000 voters in all 50 states. Younger Republican voters who supported the Republican candidate in their House race were less likely to approve of the way Trump is handling his job as president, and more likely to say he worsened the economy with his policies. About two-thirds of Republican voters under 30 said they approved of how Trump was handling the presidency, compared with about 9 in 10 Republican voters age 65 and older. About one-third of younger GOP voters said Trump had worsened the country’s economic conditions, compared with about 2 in 10 older Republican voters. The war with Iran also appeared to divide Republican voters, with about 6 in 10 Republican voters under 45 saying the U.S. made the right decision in taking military action against Iran. That rose to about 8 in 10 among Republican voters who were 45 and older. Young Republican voters were more likely to say the U.S. support for Israel was “too strong.” Roughly half of Republican voters under 30 said the country’s backing of Israel was “too strong,” compared with about 1 in 10 voters 65 and older. Despite rosy outlooks from top Republicans including Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in the final weeks of the campaign, Republican strategists had long seen the country's confidence in the party unraveling. In late August, the Senate Leadership Fund convened a donor retreat in Laguna Beach, California, where Latcham told the group that Republicans had lost the confidence of voters on handling the cost of living and the economy, according to two Republican Senate campaign sources who attended the event. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a private meeting. In defeat, Republicans are trying to take a broader view, knowing that it may take several election cycles before they one day return to power. Rep. Christopher Smith was reelected to his 24th term this week and is New Jersey's last Republican in Congress. He took a long view on the party's current struggles. “The pendulum swings back and forth,” he told reporters. “These are cycles.” ___ Associated Press writers Steve Peoples, Kevin Freking and Linley Sanders contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-grip-party-republicans-reel-124922943.html

item.title: Trump signals more cabinet changes in store after Republican midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Hegseth and Miller (AP) President Donald Trump said Friday he expects to make additional Cabinet changes following Republicans' sweeping midterm election defeats, signaling that the replacement of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles may be only the beginning of a broader administration shake-up. In an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes," Trump acknowledged that more personnel changes could be coming but declined to identify which officials might be affected. Asked whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, Trump replied, "I do, yeah. Little bit." "I love my Cabinet. I think they're good," Trump said. "But I'll ... be doing maybe a few changes." The remarks came as Trump announced Friday that longtime senior adviser Stephen Miller would replace Wiles as White House chief of staff, effective Monday. Trump's comments were made during an interview with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat scheduled to air Sunday, with excerpts released Friday. The president's remarks also come amid growing speculation about the future of War Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose handling of the war in Iran has drawn criticism following the GOP's midterm losses. CBS News reported Wednesday that Trump had privately asked advisers whether Hegseth should remain in his position, citing multiple sources familiar with the discussions. The network reported that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis had been floated as a possible replacement, although other sources said Trump had made no decision to remove Hegseth. Trump publicly expressed confidence in Hegseth when questioned Wednesday and again during the CBS interview. "I do," Trump replied Friday when asked whether he retained confidence in Hegseth. "Look, we've won two wars," the president added, referring to U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Iran. Hegseth also faces the prospect of intensified congressional scrutiny when Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Friday that Hegseth should leave office but stopped short of endorsing impeachment proceedings, according to NPR. "He's got to go," Jeffries said during an interview with NPR's "Morning Edition." Asked whether Democrats should pursue impeachment, Jeffries replied, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus." NPR also reported that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., has threatened to force a House vote on eight articles of impeachment unless Hegseth resigns. Meanwhile, Trump's decision to elevate Miller places one of his closest advisers in charge of White House operations as Democrats prepare to challenge administration policies and launch congressional investigations. CBS News reported Friday that Miller, previously deputy chief of staff, has played a central role in shaping Trump's immigration enforcement and deportation policies. His appointment could also set the stage for a more confrontational relationship with incoming Democrat congressional leaders, who have sharply criticized the administration's immigration agenda. Trump, however, rejected suggestions that Wiles' departure was prompted by the election results. "It's just time. Sometimes you change," Trump told reporters Friday, according to CNN. CBS News separately reported that Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday and that her departure was tied to the Republican election defeats, citing three sources familiar with the matter. Trump praised Miller as a trusted and effective adviser. "He's been with me right from the beginning ... he's very loyal, smart. Does a great job," Trump said, according to CNN. "He's been an MVP every year. He's been just great. So, we're very happy with him," the president added. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, has specifically identified Miller as a target for investigation. "Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct," Garcia said in a statement Friday reported by Mediaite. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," Garcia added. CBS News also reported that Garcia had singled out Miller and other administration officials as potential investigative targets following Tuesday's elections. The White House has dismissed the prospect of such inquiries as politically motivated. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News. © 2026 Newsmax. item.title: Judge wants to know if Trump officials lied about plans for his D.C. golf course
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River. Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers. The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a “World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events." An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days’ notice in writing before making any “irreparable modification” to any “forms or features” of the course while the lawsuit is active. Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled. Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government's conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys. As the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump’s 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job. Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers’ group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP. David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial's participants "can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court.” Super said it also is a reflection “of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn’t have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues.” Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on. The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real. ___ Bedayn reported from Austin, Texas. (Adds dropped word in paragraph 12) By Phil Stewart WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Building on a months-long naval blockade on Iran, the US military said on Saturday it is launching a task force to help crack ‌down on Tehran's movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material over its land borders and through the ‌Caspian Sea. Task Force Iron Gate, which was first reported by Reuters, will be based in Tampa, Florida, and will coordinate with other US government agencies. ​Beyond movement of weapons, it will also focus on halting the flow of dual-use technologies used by Iran and stemming what Washington calls illegal revenue streams. The establishment of the task force is the latest illustration of how the US is still searching for ways to increase pressure on Tehran, more than eight months after launching with Israel a war against the Islamic Republic. While US ‌strikes have dealt devastating blows to Iran's conventional ⁠military and the US naval blockade has severely restricted its crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea, Iran still poses a formidable threat to the region and its ⁠rulers have tightened their grip on the country. IRAN'S SECRET NETWORK A Reuters investigation found Iran has created a secret network of military agencies to import at least $2 billion in hardware, explosives and heavy-duty trucks since January 2025, evading both the US naval blockade and Western ​sanctions. The ​material entered Iran by cargo ship across the Caspian Sea from ​Russia, by truck from Central Asia, and by freight ‌planes from China, the Reuters investigation showed. US Central Command said the task force will coordinate with other government agencies. A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that was expected to include the Treasury, State and Justice Departments but also the intelligence community. "Strengthening CENTCOM’s collaboration with US interagency partners will further constrain Iran’s ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military," Admiral Brad Cooper, the commander of Central Command, said in a statement. Central Command estimated that its ‌naval blockade has prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in ​crude oil. Still, Iran has proven resilient and gloated following US midterm election ​results that punished Trump's Republican Party, giving control of ​Congress to opposition Democrats. Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for electoral rout, and ‌appeared to question whether the conflict was worth it. Mediators ​have intensified efforts in recent ​days to end the war between Iran and the United States amid fears it could reignite after the US midterm elections. Trump has been threatening to carry out a new offensive against Iran, putting countries in the Gulf ​on edge, since Tehran has threatened broad ‌retaliation against Gulf infrastructure. Reuters has reported that US intelligence assessments in recent months have indicated that renewed strikes ​on Iran would not fundamentally change Tehran's negotiating position or lead to the fall of Iran's government. item.title: Trump ally Laura Loomer reportedly charged up to $5,000 for political posts
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The right-wing activist Laura Loomer has been paid by private clients to make political posts on social media without publicly disclosing the payments, according to a former campaign aide to President Donald Trump and three others familiar with the arrangements, shedding light on what they say is a business practice of one of the Trump administration's most influential online firebrands. The allegations were made by Alex Bruesewitz, an adviser to Trump's 2024 campaign, and three other people who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Two of the three people said they had paid Loomer directly to post political messages on her X account, where she has 1.9 million followers. The third said they had overseen clients who paid her to post on the account. The three spoke on the condition of anonymity. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Bank transaction emails and a wire transfer statement reviewed by The Washington Post appear to show four payments totaling more than $60,000 sent to Loomer and a Florida-based company registered in her name, King Breaker Media, since May of last year. The documents do not specify the purpose of the payments, but two people familiar with the arrangements said they were for political posts. Loomer, one of Trump's best-known online acolytes, denied to The Post that she is paid to post on social media. She instead described herself as a journalist and activist and disputed the idea that she is an influencer paid to promote any political cause. The new claims about Loomer's influence business could add fuel to a growing debate about the little-regulated industry of political messaging on social media, where influencers on both sides of the aisle have operated in a legal gray area between advocacy and advertising. Bruesewitz first posted his allegations on X on Thursday. Many of the details about Loomer's alleged online influence operation have not been previously reported. Bruesewitz said in an interview with The Post that he had paid Loomer for tweets last year. He said the money had been sent through his political consulting firm, X Strategies, for posts related to policy issues. He declined to specify what clients. Despite brokering these deals himself, he believes that they should require clearer disclosures and have "gotten out of hand." Loomer disputed Bruesewitz's account and said that his firm contacted her last year offering to pay her for research. "He paid me to make a one-page research document for him, and then he wanted me to distribute the information. And that's what I did," Loomer said. Asked where she was expected to distribute the research, she said, "Either X or maybe an article." When asked how that was different from being paid to tweet, Loomer said she had actually been told to create the research document but that Bruesewitz had said he would have it distributed. Loomer accused Bruesewitz of "lashing out" at her because of her political beliefs. Bruesewitz and the three other people declined to publicly share the tweets they said Loomer had published to maintain the privacy of their clients. But The Post reviewed a selection of the tweets under the condition that they not be revealed publicly. Two of the people said that Loomer charges $3,000 to $5,000 per tweet, and sometimes more. Loomer said she does not have set pricing for consulting work. "I certainly don't charge $5,000 for a tweet," she said. The four people who had paid or oversaw payments to Loomer for posting political statements on social media said she is an effective, if sometimes unpredictable, messenger and a key way of trying to get a line directly to Trump. Jared Holt, a senior researcher at Open Measures, a platform that measures the spread of online extremism and disinformation, agreed. "This is somebody that has a tremendous amount of influence and access to the president's ear," said Holt, who studies the far right. Loomer said in an interview Thursday night that she could not discuss the terms of her work with most of her clients due to confidentiality agreements and the fact that her accountant handled her invoices. "I'm not some influencer that makes money from tweeting. My business is public affairs and opposition research," she said. "I also have a media company. It's not illegal to make a living in America." Roughly one hour after The Post discussed the claims with Loomer, she announced on X that she is taking a hiatus from her online show, "Loomer Unleashed," so she could pursue a more "healthy work life balance" and prepare for her upcoming wedding. "I just need to step back, recharge, refocus, and be present in my own life and my own mind with peace and clarity for a little while," she wrote. Loomer said the announcement had been scheduled in advance. Loomer, 33, has traveled with Trump and met privately with him in the Oval Office during his second term in office. Detractors within the administration have taken issue with Loomer's relationship to the president and have lamented that several high-ranking defense and national security officials have been dismissed after she has publicly rebuked them, often on her X account. Trump last year called Loomer a "very nice person" and a "patriot." After the White House fired aides on the National Security Council staff last year whom Loomer had accused of disloyalty, Trump denied that she was involved in the dismissal but acknowledged she had made some firing recommendations and said, "Sometimes I listen to those recommendations." The White House declined to comment. The Federal Trade Commission requires bloggers, influencers and other online figures to disclose when they have been paid to endorse a product, but the agency doesn't have jurisdiction over political ads. Some advocacy groups have called for stronger regulations around paid political content. The Campaign Legal Center last year petitioned the Federal Election Commission to consider requiring "paid for by" disclosures on influencers' political posts, saying they could help voters better assess the content they see online. California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed legislation that will penalize influencers who post paid political messages without disclosure. The general lack of transparency among political influencers, Holt said, "further degrades confidence in what people see online and how genuine it may be, or how representative it may actually be of the communities that these various influencers purport to speak for." Loomer has frequently said her bulldog advocacy reflects her genuine views, telling The Bulwark in May 2025 that she was "not paid for [her] posts." One person who said they had paid Loomer to tweet on behalf of clients said she was deliberate in her work and would only tweet if she agreed with the position. The person said not every client wanted to work with her because they believed she was polarizing but that some had hired her assuming she had an audience in the White House. The person added, however, that Loomer was like a "nuclear bomb." "You have to be careful how to use that," they said. "It's effective but also turns a lot of things to s--- if you're not careful." Loomer said she took that as a compliment. "I'm glad people find me to be effective and think I have a good reach," she said. "I'm not going to apologize for monetizing the fact that people fear me." item.title: Democrats' midterm wins could change how we elect presidents by 2028
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Could this year's big blue midterm wave transform how America elects its next president? Now that Democrats have won complete control of governor's mansions and both legislative chambers in five battleground states — Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada and Arizona — there is a chance that the Electoral College, as we know it, could soon become a thing of the past. That isn't speculation. In fact, the plan is already in motion. Over the last two decades, 18 states and Washington, D.C., have formally agreed to award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential ticket wins the most votes nationwide, regardless of the outcome in their own state or district. Until now, this legal agreement — official name: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) — hasn't taken effect because the jurisdictions that have joined it only control 222 total electoral votes, which falls short of the 270 required to activate the compact (and elect a president). But what if you add Pennsylvania (19 electoral votes), Michigan (15), Arizona (11), Wisconsin (10) and Nevada (6) to the list? That gets you to 283 (assuming that all of them join and the compact survives potential constitutional challenges). Since Election Day, the Democratic shift in statehouses across the country has been overshadowed by the massive Democratic shift on Capitol Hill . But as the dust settles, attention is turning toward a new possibility: that a handful of states might suddenly have the power to ensure that whoever wins the national popular vote in 2028 will also win the presidency (which hasn't always been the case ). "The time is right," Carrie Rheingans, a Democrat in the Michigan House of Representatives, told the New York Times this week . "This blue tsunami is really going to help push this forward across the whole nation." "National popular vote will be something that we'll prioritize early in the session," added Kelda Roys, a Democratic state lawmaker in Wisconsin. Here's everything you need to know about the national popular vote compact — and its chances of taking effect. How does the Electoral College currently work? The Electoral College is a system of indirect democracy in which the winner of the U.S. presidential election is determined not by the combined number of votes a candidate has earned across all states — aka the "popular vote" — but rather by the number of "electoral votes" they've amassed by winning in individual states. With minor exceptions, the candidate who gets the most votes in a particular state on Election Day is awarded all of that state's electoral votes, which match the number of senators and representatives it sends to Congress. Whichever presidential ticket secures a majority of electoral votes — that is, 270 — wins. Due to the winner-take-all nature of the Electoral College, candidates tend not to campaign in states that consistently vote Democratic (blue states) or Republican (red states). Instead, they focus on the small number of states (known as swing states, battleground states, toss-up states or purple states) that could go one way or the other. The Founding Fathers established the Electoral College in the Constitution. Some of them wanted qualified citizens to elect the president by popular vote; others wanted Congress to elect the president. The Electoral College was the compromise they landed on. Today's Electoral College system evolved over time as individual states passed their own winner-take-all laws. But the Founders never specified how electors — the ones who cast the electoral votes — would be appointed. Instead, the Constitution explicitly delegates that power to the states themselves, saying they can choose their electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." National popular vote advocates argue that this clause gives state lawmakers " a built-in way to reform the system ." How could the national popular vote compact change America's presidential elections? Prior to the 20th century, three presidents won the White House without winning the popular vote: John Quincy Adams in 1824, Rutherford B. Hayes in 1876 and Benjamin Harrison in 1888. But the idea for a national popular vote compact only started to gain traction among scholars after George W. Bush lost the popular vote in 2000 and wound up in the White House anyway. Sixteen years later, Trump's popular-vote loss to Hillary Clinton — by a margin of nearly 3 million ballots — added more fuel to the fire. The Bush and Trump victories also polarized the issue, making Democrats more open to the idea of reform — and Republicans more opposed (in general). The NPVIC was introduced in 2006 by John Koza , a computer scientist and former Democratic elector who co-invented the lottery scratchcard. The idea is simple. First, individual states agree to award all of their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote. When enough states agree — that is, enough states with a combined total of at least 270 electoral votes — then the compact will take effect and the candidate who earns the most popular votes nationwide will be guaranteed enough electoral votes to win the White House. No constitutional amendment required. National popular vote proponents say that their plan will completely change the way candidates campaign for (and even govern as) president. Rather than lavishing all their time, energy and resources on a small handful of swing states, aspiring commanders in chief would in theory have to cater to voters everywhere in hopes of maximizing their nationwide vote tally. In April 2007, Maryland became the first state to sign on. Ten more jurisdictions followed suit before the 2016 election (California, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and the District of Columbia), with another eight joining the compact after Trump became president (Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon and Virginia). Republican-led chambers have adopted the NPVIC in New York (2011), Oklahoma (2014) and Arizona (2016) — but generally, Democrats have needed complete statehouse control to enact it into law. Which is where Democrats' shiny new trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada come into play. What's next According to the Times, "lawmakers in key states said on Thursday that they had already begun having conversations this week about introducing legislation to join the agreement in the next session, and were hopeful that they would succeed ahead of 2028." But hopeful doesn't mean certain. One of the new trifecta states, Michigan, failed to get over the line during its previous Democratic trifecta, from 2023 to 2024 — and Nevada fell short in 2019 when its then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact amid fears it could diminish his small state's outsized influence over presidential elections. Virginia became the most recent state to join the compact after Democrats there won a trifecta in 2025. Republicans called the move an " unconstitutional assault on our democracy ," arguing it undermines the influence of Virginia voters. One major question is whether lawmakers will prioritize the national popular vote after campaigning in 2026 on more visceral issues like lowering the cost of living. "Time will tell," Clinton Anderson, a Democratic state assemblyman in Wisconsin, told the Times. "I want to make it a priority, but it's not the thing I heard on the doors I knocked." Another question is what might happen in the courts if the compact actually kicks in. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the NPVIC would be unconstitutional without congressional approval — which, in his view, is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause. "It's a very real possibility that enough states join this compact," Muller told the Times. But, he added, "there will be a lot of challenges." item.title: The Trump admin wants underwater data centers. 1 non-profit is already preparing.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The skyline of Cleveland, Ohio, on 30 September 2023. Photograph: Photo by Mike Kline (notkalvin)/Getty Images While Elon Musk has often touted putting datacenters in space, reports suggest that another geographic area may soon become a widespread target: our lakes and oceans . Two underwater datacenters are already in operation off the coast of China, and recent reports suggest that the Trump administration is considering plans for four proposed underwater, sealed-pod datacenters to be built off the shores of Maine and Alaska . At a campaign rally in Ohio last month, Donald Trump said of datacenters: “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio … they’ll go to China … we want them.” Underwater iterations are particularly attractive to tech companies as they largely eliminate community opposition and controversy around datacenters in residential areas on land. In theory, underwater datacenters could also significantly cut down on utility costs, another issue that’s currently riling communities across the country. A Microsoft project set up off the coast of northern Scotland in 2018 found that after two years, server failures were reduced by 87% compared with on-land datacenter equivalents. Microsoft executives saw the project, which ended after two years, as an unmitigated success. That makes the cool, salt-free waters of the Great Lakes, home to 30 million people in major cities such as Chicago, Toronto and Detroit, potentially attractive to datacenter companies. A spokesperson for the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said: “The EPA supports development of data center infrastructure that is essential to remaining the world leader in Super Intelligence while using its statutory authorities to protect water quality.” But the environmental consequences of any similar project in the freshwater Great Lakes, which those tens of millions of people depend on for drinking water every day, could be significant. Local environmental activists are already worried and sounding the alarm – even though no underwater datacenter projects are currently proposed for the region. For them, they think it is better to be prepared than surprised, given the high stakes of the ecologically sensitive ecosystem. “We are concerned because if you think about what a datacenter does, it throws off a lot of heat. Lake Erie already has an issue with harmful algal blooms, and they develop because of heat, not only because of fertilizers and agricultural runoff,” said John Lipaj of the Lake Erie Foundation , a non-profit based in Ohio. The floor of Lake Erie on the US side falls under the jurisdiction of the state of Ohio. In the past, its state government, where Republicans hold a supermajority, proposed a law making it easier for datacenter companies to discharge wastewater into public waterways. That measure was denied by the state’s EPA last July following a public outcry. Of the eight US Great Lakes states, only New York currently has a temporary state-wide moratorium on datacenter construction. That ends in mid-2027. “We’re also concerned about the possibility of contamination and leaks. These have not been around a long time,” said Lipaj. “We are concerned about the types of fluid contained in a datacenter, the batteries and electrical equipment. These are all things that could lead to a catastrophic failure that we don’t want happening in the Great Lakes.” Lake Erie is home or close to major cities such as Cleveland, Detroit and Buffalo and is already by far the warmest of the five Great Lakes during summer months. It also ranks as one of the most polluted large lakes in the country in large part due to agricultural runoff in its western basin. A number of fish species are under threat due to the lake’s warming trend. “Warm water can impact aquatic life and ecosystems in a number of ways. One immediate effect is what is known as a thermal shock,” said Helena Volzer of the Alliance for the Great Lakes, an environmental group based in Chicago. “Aquatic organisms are highly sensitive to temperature changes, and even a small, rapid increase of just 2-5F can be dramatic for the aquatic ecosystem. When a facility releases warm water, it can alter metabolism and increase oxygen demand, reduce dissolved oxygen availability, disrupt food webs [and] force fish to move away from preferred habitats.” On 3 November, residents of Conneaut, a Lake Erie community of about 12,000 people an hour’s drive north-east of Cleveland, voted in favor of a charter amendment to prohibit the construction of large datacenters in its area. But the idea of offshore underwater datacenters is not a popular one here. “Being one of the largest freshwater sources in the world, I would be very much for protecting that resource,” said Mariana Branch, a Conneaut council member who lives a short distance from the Lake Erie shoreline. Branch said she hadn’t previously been aware of the idea of datacenters operating underwater. “Technology is moving so quickly, it’s difficult for cities to keep up with,” she said. Still, some suggest that following Microsoft’s lead in Scotland may have some merit considering the public opposition to on-land equivalents; and, unlike the open ocean, there are no large fauna in the Great Lakes ecosystems. “They require a lot of energy for cooling … one of the biggest advantages of these underwater datacenters is the low cooling cost [associated]. They don’t have to spend a lot to cool the servers,” said Nir Kshetri, a professor of emerging technologies at the University of North Carolina Greensboro. “Datacenters have been a big issue for communities and in the recent elections. Also, datacenters don’t have to worry about any latency problems because they can be located close to large population centers where they are needed. A lake is a great place to do a datacenter. Cold water is even better.” However, the Great Lakes are not without significant challenges to any such project. Last winter saw one of the most extensive Great Lakes freeze-ups in decades, with almost all of Lake Erie and up to half of the four other lakes freezing over up to several feet deep. Experts say it isn’t clear to what extent ice cover could affect underwater projects. What’s more, a Microsoft spokesperson said: “We have no plans to deploy an underwater datacenter in any location at this time,” and: “Our focus today is on building and operating datacenters responsibly on land.” A spokesperson for Ohio’s EPA said it had not yet received any applications to permit an underwater datacenter in its part of Lake Erie. For its part, Lipaj says the Lake Erie Foundation has contacted state representatives and state senators in New York, Ohio and Michigan to discuss the issue. “Whether or not they happen, [we’re saying] let’s propose to state legislatures in Great Lakes states that they consider that this may be coming down the line and let’s get some regulations in place before the datacenter developers make their proposals and then state legislators are scrambling. That’s what we’re trying to avoid. We’re exercising an abundance of caution,” he said. “The Great Lakes states should take some leadership in this, get the regulations written so that nothing is forced on them.” This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/trump-administration-wants-underwater-datacenters-140014506.html

item.title: Egypt reopens embassy in Libya's Tripoli after 12-year closure
item.description:
Source: Straits Times World (Global)
TRIPOLI, Nov 7 - Egypt reopened its embassy in Libya's capital Tripoli on Saturday after a 12-year absence, marking a rapprochement with the country's western-based administration, the foreign affairs ministry in Cairo said in a statement.
